notes.title: Nominate Torn Away for the Steam Awards
notes.notes:
Torn Away is an emotional adventure about a ten-year-old girl who is a victim of labour slavery during World War II.

We spent a lot of time studying archival materials and even consulted an expert historian from the international human rights organisation Memorial, which won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.

With care and respect, we made Asya's journey heartbreaking, historically accurate, and understandable to players from any place on Earth. Play for sure!

If you've played Torn Away, [b]please nominate Torn Away for Outstanding Story-Rich Game[/b].
Your support is priceless.

notes.title: Why is Torn Away a 2.5D game?
notes.notes:
[previewyoutube=NxZWVqAp1u0;full][/previewyoutube]

This is how our developers see the 2.5D game inside the Unity3D!

A few years ago we decided to make a 3D game with 2D sprites of characters and hand-drawn textures. Such complications allowed us to make a variety of gameplay in one unique style. Thanks to the unity of the visual style, the transition from third-person view to first-person view feels like an interesting effect, rather than a switch between two different games. The game's brilliant final visuals are the result of shaders, particles, and the work of tech art team.

notes.title: Polishing: new animations
notes.notes:
[previewyoutube=jkeKNOSyUio;full][/previewyoutube]

What is the main problem with integrating new animations into the game? One word: bugs. But the result is worth it. After all, the game experience is made up of many small details. 

In the old version, Asya could only run on a log. This funny, almost cartoonish animation looks unrealistic if the player didn't speed up before climbing the log. We added idle animation and the ability to walk cautiously. When Asya freezes in indecision and tries to find her balance, the player realizes that the surface of the tree may be uneven or slippery. Asya is afraid to fall, but she has only one way to go — forward.

notes.title: How Torn Away's tone has changed
notes.notes:
For story-driven games is important not only the plot and dialogue, but the overall mood. It cannot be described in the terms of reference or tested with a simple prototype.

First playable demo of Torn Away was grim. In this version, Asya found a new friend, Zoya. 
Zoya died.
The game was scary, but it wasn't the fun fear of the usual horror games.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40400192/f550919cc6bdb2d4de091fa83d4c9f47fe02c54d.gif[/img]


We decided that a story about a child should have more inspirational episodes. And the playtests of the new version of Torn Away proved us right. Players experience stronger emotions if the game has a contrast of somber and touching episodes. We ourselves like to create games that help players believe that everything is going to be okay.

notes.title: Development log 4: Lightning and Animation
notes.notes:
Hello, and welcome back, to our newest devlog!

Today we will talk about creating animations in our game. Animation in a broad sense is any dynamics on the scene. But here, we divide everything into several aspects: character animation, cutscenes animation and technical animation.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/BkQXVAY.gif[/img]

There is only one animator in our studio and Torn Away was a huge challenge for him. When we first started working on the game, no one could have imagined that the number of all animations would become so huge. Add here an almost complete restart — when we heavily redesigned the main character — and you will understand his pain!

Despite the fact that the animator's experience was mainly in frame-by-frame animation, we jointly decided that we would do skeletal 2d animation in the Spine software.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/cscqjdw.gif[/img]

This made the whole process more flexible and customizable. For example, we can remove certain items of clothing without having to redraw all the frames again. This can be done on the engine side.
The same works for the emotions on the girl's face. We can change them, regardless of the movement of the body.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/ThVUsXn.gif[/img]

Even though we're doing skeletal animation, the experience of frame-by-frame animation helped us create more lifelike motion. Here you can see how for the animation of running and falling, the linear version was first performed, and then the final one in Spine

[img]https://i.imgur.com/JdUycwA.gif[/img]

Choosing the right tool and approach is a vital part of any development process. It is important to explore all the possibilities in order to understand which one will be the most optimal.
For example, at a certain stage of development, we considered the possibility of transferring the character to 3D. Thus, it would be more convenient for us to build interactions with a three-dimensional environment.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/iZq2oTi.png[/img]

But our animator had no experience in 3D animation, and the character himself turned out to be not as expressive as his 2D ancestor.

We share the first tests of 3D animation using the free Mixamo service, and trained Asya to fight, just for this one occurrence ;)

[img]https://i.imgur.com/Mx6I55F.gif[/img]

We also planned to make several different death screens using animation presets. But later we realized that we would not pull the production of truly diverse and interesting screens. The idea had to be abandoned.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/VelJbvP.gif[/img]

Speaking about other ideas that had to be abandoned, I would like to recall the animation of the hands when viewed from the first person. As planned, in all or most of the mini-games, we had to see the hands of the main character. Here is one of the first prototypes.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/Z7jwX66.gif[/img]

But doing them all in 3D would be really expensive, and the 2D animation wasn't that convincing.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/v8Yr0Wi.gif[/img]

I would like to say a few words about the iterative approach in creating dramatic moments in scenes.
The main difficulty when working with them is that it is important for us to convey the idea using a visual language - graphics and animation. But at the same time, we want the player not to spoil the dramatic moment for themselves by doing something wrong. Therefore, we have to find a balance between interactivity and prepared animations.

The process usually starts with a script and a rough storyboard.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/SHFgOMB.png[/img]

Then a concept that sets the mood.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/1EEyDxz.jpg[/img]

Next, we block out and try to understand how it will look in dynamics.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/Qzx5Uos.gif[/img]

Then in color.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/ZxtF8Fv.gif[/img]

After all of this, the finish line is a stone's throw away! In theory. In practicality, there were many more iterations, especially a lot of time is spent on character animation and coordination of all elements together.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/RWW4nsR.gif[/img]

And if in scenes like the previous one, the emphasis is on beautiful graphics and character animation, then in first-person scenes, technical art (shaders, particle systems) and well-thought-out level design rule.

Here you can see some of the internals of the blizzard scene.

[img]http://i.imgur.com/EtRX0lGh.gif[/img]

After a few experiments, our game designer and programmer managed to get the right feel for this scene. Cold and helplessness is what we strived for, so we keep pressing on!

Yes, for an unprepared viewer, it looks very sketchy, but our artists immediately see how to bring this scene to a finished look.

[img]http://i.imgur.com/AmOoYlmh.gif[/img]

What this location looks like now you'll just have to find out for yourself, but for now I'm leaving you with a tiny teaser ;)

[img]https://i.imgur.com/iNZjJJS.jpg[/img]

We often wondered: maybe we should have made a simple game, focusing only on 2D graphics?
But doing different experiments with each scene, we understood that our path, however difficult, is worth it.

The possibilities that open up for setting up light, materials, angles are simply breathtaking.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/kW29yOD.gif[/img]

[img]https://i.imgur.com/Tg4rH4R.gif[/img]

[img]https://i.imgur.com/nL5Ssgf.gif[/img]

Nevertheless, no matter how exciting our experiments with technical art are, we do not forget about the emotion evoked by hand-drawn graphics. Our story is filled with dozens of painstakingly drawn illustrations, which we brought to life with the help of the previously voiced Spine.

Here too, everything starts with rough storyboards.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/w8OAqoB.png[/img]

Then comes the stage of preparing illustrations.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/cE7IaVk.jpg[/img]

Well, in the end - the detailing of graphics and animation. The scene comes to life.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/6NJA1b0.gif[/img]

Here I also want to share a few sketches of frame-by-frame animation. Such sketches often help us find the right mood for a particular scene.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/Hq8rsRk.gif[/img]

We hope you enjoyed today's story as much as the previous ones!

See you soon!

[img]https://i.imgur.com/9EFPHB1.gif[/img]

notes.title: Torn Away Development Log #3: The World
notes.notes:
[img]https://i.imgur.com/cNTNES0.jpg[/img]

When you look at the huge amount of work that has been accomplished in two and a half years, you would not believe that this was possible at the first place. But the point is that nothing happens right away - the creation of the game world, like any other complex aspect, is a long road of small steps.
So, today we will tell you about how the style and visual language of Torn Away locations were formed.
It all started with the first mood sketches. Even when the script and storylines weren't ready yet, we tried to find what kind of mood we wanted to convey.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/7r9Cz59.jpg[/img]

The purpose of the thumbnail sketch is to establish composition and tone relationships at the level of several spots. For some locations, we made such a sketch right in 3d space using the grease pencil tool right in Blender. This allows us not only to establish tonal relationships and composition, but also to immediately understand how the parallax of our sprites will work.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/QIrwdaG.gif[/img]

In the process of searching, the graphic style of the game developed and changed beyond recognition. This happened for several reasons - for example, testing technologies: for our art director, it was important that the solutions conceived in graphic editors could be implemented in the engine.
Character design also influenced the overall style. If at first it was cute and stylized, as we went on we came to more realistic proportions, leaving a certain amount of convention. This was necessary for the design to work well in conjunction with the content of the story and the emotion that we want to convey. The overall minimalism of the presentation was necessary so that the project, in principle, was feasible for our small team. We didn't have a huge budget like Ori, where each sprite was drawn for a long time and painstakingly by experienced artisans. Therefore, we chose such a presentation, where we could put together effective working compositions from simple fills and texture strokes without wasting a lot of time.

A clear evolution of style.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/RmpjBuv.jpg[/img]

[img]https://i.imgur.com/n3WdG7z.jpg[/img]


And more steps.

[previewyoutube=c7S6A6eaUfw;full][/previewyoutube]

When the main style is set, an understandable, but at the same time no less difficult part of the work remains - thinking over each location and then gradually working out the graphics. The process for everyone is about the same - general sketching, blocking, object concepts - working out 2D and 3D assets, drawing textures and then final assembly of the level in the editor.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/9TODr53.jpg[/img]

[img]https://i.imgur.com/sPWAtBu.png[/img]

[img]https://i.imgur.com/9RFxCzn.jpg[/img]


Even though Torn Away is a war game, we didn't want our scenes to feel drab and dark. Firstly, our heroine Asya is a child, and we wanted to show that even in the most terrible conditions, children do not lose their special view of the world. And secondly, the contrast allows us to evoke the most vivid emotions in the player.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/1LS3gMW.jpg[/img]


Below is the process of working on the forest level.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/zBCGYJL.png[/img]

[img]https://i.imgur.com/efDLhuO.png[/img]

[previewyoutube=DCriHLnQ3Lg;full][/previewyoutube]

Now this level looks like this.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/iA0Kb2z.jpg[/img]

[previewyoutube=JT6S4CfrvLk;full][/previewyoutube]

In addition to visual expressiveness, it was also very important for us to maintain historical accuracy. Yes, of course, we stylize images from references, but knowledgeable people will be able to find out what was the source of inspiration for this or that object.
The location of the German city that Asya wanders into has become one of the most difficult for us. We did not take any particular city as a basis, but tried to convey the spirit of small German towns of that period.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/MIeGkVi.jpg[/img]

[previewyoutube=hGOAcfR1vs8;full][/previewyoutube]

You can see several propaganda posters here. Upon closer inspection, it becomes clear that we did not use real Nazi symbols. Some countries have laws that prohibit the use of such symbols even in historical works of art. We decided that it is more important for us to convey the spirit of that time than to portray real posters.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/ZsDwfnQ.jpg[/img]

It was much easier for us to work on Soviet interiors. Since we ourselves are from Russia, we know where and how to find the necessary materials. There are many museums dedicated to this period that carefully collect items from the early and mid-20th centuries. Among other things, we know and love Soviet films, which also have enough historically correct sets.
It's always a pleasure to look to your country's culture for inspiration.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/neDHRrq.png[/img]

[img]https://i.imgur.com/8cxY9J9.jpg[/img]

Looking at archival materials and footage from old films, it is difficult to imagine that Asya's room could look like this - bright and cheerful. As if there is no and will not be any war.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/v8eu7ZO.jpg[/img]

Thank you for delving into this trip down our development ‘memory’ road with us. We have oh so much in store for you, so please, let us know your thoughts and stay tuned!

notes.title: Torn Away Development Log #2: Stealth
notes.notes:
[h1]Hey everyone! [/h1]



Today, we’re going to talk about the development process of one of our gameplay systems, namely Stealth.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40400192/f3b3433a1c484d4ddab102b46450665c1dbad736.jpg[/img]


During the development process, we tried quite a few different mechanics: some of them we kept since they worked well; some just did not feel right for the game and had to be abandoned. I want to point out that, while developing the game, we prioritised the story first and our primary goal was to choose mechanics that would support the narrative.

We understood this was not the easiest approach, but felt the consequences and complexity of it wayyy after the development was already underway. We do not recommend doing this :D Of course, now we have found our footing and do not have any regrets about this approach.

So, shrugging aside the fact that we started from the narrative, we had a wide variety of other difficulties, a majority of which were dictated by the story itself. For example, as you know, our main character is the girl Asya, who, due to her age and character, cannot and does not want to fight. For a war game, the inability to use combat mechanics is quite a challenge... Another challenge is the realistic historical setting. No portal guns and flying robots! You get it.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40400192/51212c7546547ae7b6e4c73f2a5c96fd2699fdf0.jpg[/img]


Of course, there are other narrative games out there and somehow they get by just fine. But the fact is that our story is set during a war, which means that creating tangible tension is still a challenge that we NEED to overcome.

This is how we came to the stealth mechanic.

We knew right away that stealth in our game would be pretty simple. It was very important for the team to make sure that stealth in the game is not as nuanced like in other games that rely more on the mechanic like Metal Gear Solid, but still keep the player engaged and invested in completing the level. After all, we primarily have a narrative game and storytelling is our priority.


[img]https://thumbs.gfycat.com/BareFewBilby-size_restricted.gif[/img]


The mechanics of basic stealth were a piece of cake. But the main issue was that it was near impossible for us to predict if the player response was going to be on a par with what we intended. Will the player believe in the reality of the situation, and won’t ‘fall out’ of the narrative?

This is generally one of the key problems when making a game with an emphasis on story: nothing is clear until the level takes on a recognizable form. No tiny nuance can be overlooked, as each plays a major role: location graphics, lights, character animations, sounds, music... but they all require veeeeery long hours of work. 

All this to say, sometimes you’ve just got to suck it up, and just do the work without knowing all the details, and judge it only after it’s done, with the whole picture in view.

Back to stealth.

Another great problem we faced was threat indication. In the prototype, we were able to use indicators that everyone understands like "green = safe, red = dangerous". But this was incomplete and, as such, unacceptable in the finished product.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40400192/ada1723dc6fbbc3dbef585ad0a5460a25dbaf154.jpg[/img]


After a lot of trial and error, we settled on lantern light as an understandable indicator of danger. After sketching out the rough graphics, animations, and sound, we knew we were heading in the right direction.


[img]https://thumbs.gfycat.com/MasculineAptAmericanavocet-size_restricted.gif[/img]


Even though this is still far from the final result, you can clearly see that the main ideas were laid down during this period.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40400192/7c3c96af2705021bbdf401456680f7307d0a33ac.jpg[/img]


Another great idea came from our game designer, who suggested using sound to indicate danger. When the light of the lantern passes next to Asya, you can hear a crackle that indicates a light source close by. Of course, "light" has no sound in real life, but such a sound effect allows a certain feeling of immersion to be experienced. Sounds crazy, but it really works!


[previewyoutube=-aLZZ_3Kpak;full][/previewyoutube]
From a technical point of view, it works like this. There is a trigger (or several triggers), which have a link to the object of danger - in this case, a soldier. For each trigger, the viewing angle and time are set. If the player is in the trigger and enters the soldier's view within the specified time, Asya gets caught and you are taken back to the start of the level.

If the player is in the trigger, but outside the soldiers’ field of vision, then the timer gradually decreases to zero, and gives Asya some time to escape.

In parallel, a separate state can be set for the object of danger. He does not have to stand and look near the trigger, he can walk and go about his business. And after entering the trigger, this state changes.

Even with such a simple system, it is possible to make places where you cannot raise your head above the shelter. To make this happen, we just placed the trigger above the character.
Although this is not a systemic approach (like a sensor system), it allows us to conveniently set up and direct stealth sections.


[previewyoutube=jneMVigkUS8;full][/previewyoutube]
At the end of the day, it is up to you to judge whether we succeeded in implementing all of these systems. We can only promise that we still have some tricks up our sleeves when it comes to this mechanic. We hope you have fun figuring it all out when the game releases!

================================================================================


Thank you for your support, we have much more content for you, so stay tuned for our upcoming DevLogs ;)

notes.title: Torn Away Development Log #1: Asya
notes.notes:
Hey everyone, and welcome, to the first ever Torn Away development log!

With each passing day our enthusiasm about Torn Away grows, and sometimes, we have to let some of it out, before the developer team explodes!
This is our way of showing that enthusiasm - a devlog about Asya, the main protagonist of our game, Torn Away. Hopefully after reading this piece, you’ll have a deeper understanding of some of our design choices while developing a relatable and empathetic protagonist, and their way of coping with situations no-one should ever experience.

So, Asya.  

[img]https://i.imgur.com/diSOqAt.gif[/img]

At first, Asya can seem like a stereotypical schoolgirl, however reality is anything but. While well-mannered and enthusiastic, Asya has an extremely complicated personal life. She has no close friends and her home life is definitely not perfect — her father went to the Front to fight for his country and family, and her mother has to work for two, and hardly ever sees her daughter. As constant loneliness takes over Asya, she becomes more anxious and withdrawn, while still fighting back against it all in her own ways. A significant part of the game is devoted to how Asya copes with loneliness. One such tool is a personal diary.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/54YG2Rd.jpg[/img]

At the start of the development process, we poured over a ton of material we could use to bring our idea to reality. One of the main examples we used was the widely known Anne Frank’s diary, but as we kept doing our research, we found out that there were many children who kept diaries as they also went through the war. While working on this idea, we found a huge source of inspiration - a book with notes from diaries of Soviet children written during the second World War. Some of the stories we found there shook us to our core. One of these notes mentioned them surviving the blockade of Leningrad, and finding themselves in the middle of a hostile territory. Events like these become ingrained in you, and keeping a detailed diary is one of the more effective ways to comprehend the incredibly intense situations you were placed in, and help you remain sane in the face of adversity on this scale.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/Q9KvMlp.jpg[/img]

We thought about taking a person from the diaries and trying our best to tell their story in the game, but quickly realised this was a very wrong idea. There were many hoops to jump through, from getting permission, to the immense weight of responsibility of telling the story right, and respecting the victims. Looking at these and many more factors, we decided to use the diaries as an inspiration for an fictional, yet original and authentic story that both respects the history and it’s victims, and serves as an experience players like you would want to try. 

[b]And all of this leads back to Asya.[/b]

We decided to design Asya not as a specific hero, but a collective image, an amalgam of what we thought the children that wrote the diaries we talked about earlier looked like. At first, the girl did not have a name, her age was constantly changing during the development and writing of the script. We experimented, drew different variations, argued, looked at a ton of references, and started all over again. There were an incredible amount of iterations, but if you looked closer for a second, you’d see that Asya did not change that drastically with each version, it was more like we were taking tiny steps to our final destination, it being the Asya you can see in the trailers now.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/2DNHviB.jpg[/img]

It's hard to believe now, but we got to the final image only after six months of work. We worked around the clock to make sure Asya is as fleshed out as possible, as well as able to connect with a player on an emotional level not only through her emotions, but her appearance as well.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/s8W2b16.png[/img]

As your journey with Asya goes on, she will not only change as a person, but her changes will also be reflected in her appearance as well. This is a tough task for our artists and animators, but we feel that focusing on following Asya’s journey through her appearance will allow us to tell the story on multiple different levels, and add the level of detail that most of you (we hope) will enjoy.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/WtPewMh.png[/img]

A separate challenge for us was to create not only a stylized character for the game scenes, but also to achieve a strong image in the animated cutscenes that will feature at the end of each chapter. We simply cannot wait for you to see them in all of their beauty.

[img]https://i.imgur.com/a8Uamwz.png[/img]

This marks the end of our devlog. We want you to know that we really really appreciate the love you guys have been showing Asya on our social media. It warms our hearts to know that what we do is meaningful, and evokes the most positive of emotions from players all around the world. 

Thank you again and we hope to see you when we release more content like this in the future! <3

notes.title: Torn Away at the Steam Next Fest!
notes.notes:
Hello!

We are delighted to announce that [b]Torn Away[/b] will be accessible for the players to enjoy during this year’s Steam Next Fest. After a successful Gamescom, the demo will be available once again for players to get a taste of this genre-defying experience across war-torn Europe.

Alongside the demo, you'll be able to join us in a few let's play sessions with different team members, where they will talk about the development process, artistic and story directions.

While [b]Torn Away[/b] is still a work in progress and is constantly being tweaked, we feel both of these events will give you a good understanding of the choices we made, why we made them, and, most importantly, how the game looks and feels to play. Currently, our team at Perelesoq is hard at work incorporating voice-overs into the game to create not only a realistic but also a more immersive final version of the game. 

We hope you have a great time enjoying the experience, and please stay tuned for more news about [b]Torn Away[/b] in the near future!
